stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin Will Hold Their First Three-Way Meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November
stories.what_happened: The White House said on Friday 13 November, and the Kremlin confirmed on Saturday 14 November, that US President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin will meet together on Thursday 19 November in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Officials say Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and about the Iran war; Ukraine is not expected to be discussed. A senior US official said no agreement is expected and called the meeting the start of a conversation.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the first time the three leaders have met together, and it comes nine months after the last treaty limiting US and Russian nuclear weapons expired.

key_facts.fact: On Friday 13 November 2026 the White House said President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting will take place on Thursday 19 November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.
The Kremlin confirmed the meeting on Saturday 14 November.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russia's Tass news agency: 'This meeting will take place in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit.' The APEC summit runs on 18 and 19 November.
The White House called the three-way meeting 'unprecedented'.
Wales said: 'The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world.'
Trump says the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles.
A senior US official said the president 'does intend to talk about Iran' at the three-way meeting.
Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be discussed. The US official said Washington is running a separate negotiating track with Kyiv and Moscow, and that China is not part of that track.
A senior Trump administration official told Reuters: 'We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement.' The official described the meeting as the start of a conversation.
New START, the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow, lapsed in February 2026, nine months before the meeting.
With New START expired, the United States and Russia, which hold the largest atomic arsenals, have no limits on their stockpiles for the first time in more than 50 years.
Trump rejected Russia's proposal to extend New START by one year and demanded a 'new, improved and modernised' deal that includes China.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the United States, then China.
Pentagon estimates put China's arsenal above 600 warheads. The United States and Russia are each estimated to have more than 5,000.
China has shown little interest in a nuclear pact, given its much smaller stockpile.

Commentators have compared the planned meeting to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four occupation zones and finalised plans for the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the Yalta comparison, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on other countries.

Peskov said: 'It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant.' He added that a global order should rest on mutual benefit and mutual respect, not on any one power imposing its view.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.
Trump will also hold a separate working lunch and meeting with Xi on Thursday; it will be their fourth meeting since Trump returned to power last year.
Trump leaves Washington on Monday 16 November and arrives in the Philippines on Tuesday 17 November for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.
Elon Musk, the head of Tesla and SpaceX, will travel with Trump to China but will not take part in the meeting with Xi and Putin.
US export controls on sensitive chip technology are not expected to come up. A second US official said: 'We do not negotiate American export controls.'
The APEC summit brings 21 economies to Shenzhen, China's technology hub, which grew from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic centre in a few decades.
Analysts expect low odds of major breakthroughs and say the meeting will be more symbolic than substantive (Associated Press).
Trump and Putin have met in person seven times, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Putin have met more than 40 times since 2013.
China is Russia's top trading partner. China says it is neutral on the war in Ukraine.

The United States is at war with Iran; Trump and Xi have differed over it, and Russia has deepened its partnership with Iran. Analysts say the rise in global crude oil prices is mostly due to the Iran war.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said earlier that Russia and the US had not agreed on a separate two-way meeting between Putin and Trump on the sidelines.

stories.headline: A Router Overload Halts Every US Flight Departure for More Than Four Hours; Recovery Takes the Whole Weekend
stories.what_happened: On Friday 13 November the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop, pausing all departures across the country for more than four hours after radar and communications at air traffic control centres became unstable. Officials traced it to a newly switched-on router at a remote site in El Dorado, Arkansas, part of work to replace copper lines with fibre; no cyberattack was found. More than 17,500 flights were cancelled on Friday and Saturday, nearly 2,300 more on Sunday, and officials expected normal operations by Monday 16 November.
stories.why_it_matters: It showed how much of daily life depends on old equipment working without a break, and it started an argument in Washington over who pays to replace the air traffic control system.

key_facts.fact: Shortly after 3:30 p.m. Eastern time on Friday 13 November 2026 the FAA began experiencing 'instability for our radar and communications', Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
At 3:54 p.m. the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, pausing all departures across the country. Duffy said 3,500 planes were in the air at the time.
The ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m., after more than four hours.
Flights already in the air were allowed to reach their destinations; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said more than 3,000 aircraft landed safely during the disruption.
The FAA said all flights were halted 'out of an abundance of caution' and that every flight was accounted for. It said: 'Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems.'
It was only the second nationwide ground stop since 11 September 2001. The previous one was in 2023, when an FAA system that gives pilots safety notices before departure went down.
Instability hit 17 of the 22 en route air traffic control centres. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said none of the facilities actually went dark.
The problem first appeared as static at the Indianapolis centre. It took about 45 minutes to trace, partly because maintenance is logged on paper.
Nick Daniels, president of the air traffic controllers' union NATCA, said communications with some planes were disrupted and controllers moved flights to working radio frequencies.

The outage began with work to switch lines from copper to fibre at a remote FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Duffy said that when a new router there was turned on, a router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, installed about three weeks earlier, 'started to flood our system as well'.
Duffy said: 'Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data ... and started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.'

Officials believe a feature that broadcast data more widely than necessary caused the overload. The FAA has disabled it on all 69 routers of that type in the national airspace system, and Duffy said that resolved the issue.

Officials do not yet know whether the router was defective or whether the contractor, L3Harris, installed or configured it incorrectly. The FAA is working with the FBI, and both routers are being examined at an L3Harris lab in Florida.
The routers were made by Juniper, owned by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which said: 'the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly.'
Bedford said: 'We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related.' Officials found no evidence of a cyberattack.
L3Harris has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper to fibre, which Duffy says will be finished by the end of 2028.
More than 17,500 flights were cancelled on Friday and Saturday, ABC News reported.
Most days that week had about 100 flight cancellations in the United States.

On Sunday 15 November, 2,291 US flights had been cancelled by 3 p.m. Eastern time, according to the tracking service FlightAware, and about 18,689 were delayed. For Monday 16 November, 144 cancellations had been reported by Sunday afternoon.

Bedford said airlines expected 'full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday'. Duffy said on Sunday: 'we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow.'
Recovery was slow because aircraft and crews were stranded in the wrong places and had to be repositioned, and because pilots and crews have limits on how long they may work.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the stop grounded 1.5 million travellers and called it an 'unprecedented breakdown'.
Some airports ran short of parking space for aircraft; Washington's Reagan National was reported at capacity.

At the FAA's request, the 42 member states of Eurocontrol suspended departures to the United States for several hours. On Saturday morning 29 flights between London Heathrow and the US were cancelled.

Under US Transportation Department rules, a traveller whose flight is cancelled, or delayed by at least three hours, and who chooses not to fly is owed a full cash refund, even on a non-refundable ticket. Because the FAA ordered the stop, airlines generally do not owe meals or hotels for Friday's cancellations.
Several college football teams, including Auburn and Purdue, travelled to their games by bus instead of flying.
Cargo was also affected: US airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods a day, according to the industry group Airlines for America.
Bedford said the network 'will continue to break until we replace it' and that there is 'no backup to the backup'. He apologised to travellers.

Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernise air traffic control. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy wants $50 billion; Duffy planned to send Congress a funding request on Monday 16 November.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, said Congress has given the administration what it asked for. Senator Maria Cantwell said the Senate Commerce Committee will review the communications technology problems.
Duffy said he expects the system to be 'back up and operational' for Thanksgiving travel. Thanksgiving was about a week away.
Daniels, the controllers' union president, said: 'I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things.' He noted that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases.
SpaceX launched its Starship test flight during the stop because the airspace near the Texas launch site had already been cleared.

stories.headline: Europe Picks Five Countries to Sit at the Ukraine Peace Talks, and a US Envoy Offers to Arrange Europe-Russia Contact
stories.what_happened: At a summit in Dublin on Friday 13 November, European Council President António Costa announced that Europe will be represented in the Ukraine peace talks by the EU institutions plus five countries: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. On Saturday 14 November US envoy Jared Kushner said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move the talks to the next stage, including direct contact between Europe and Moscow. Ukraine's President Zelenskyy said US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas in exchange for joining NATO.
stories.why_it_matters: Europe has asked for months to be in the room where its own security is discussed; it now has a named team, though the hardest questions about territory are still open.

key_facts.fact: European Council President António Costa announced on Friday 13 November 2026, at a press conference after an informal European Council in Dublin, that the European negotiating team will consist of the EU institutions plus the 'E5': France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom.
Costa said: 'Our principles and our positions in these negotiations remain well known.' He said the team will act in unity and close coordination with all member states.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the team as 'E5 plus EU Institutions' and said: 'We will defend both Ukraine's and Europe's interests.' She also said: 'A strong European presence is important.'

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said these countries and the European institutions will negotiate with Russia, Ukraine and the US. He said: 'At stake are peace in Ukraine and the security of Poland and all of Europe,' and 'This is our time.'

Von der Leyen said the goal is to end the war with strong security guarantees and a plan for Ukraine's recovery, and that the EU will soon propose a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia and a way to close Ukraine's 2027 financing gap.

The five countries have signalled readiness to send troops in a 'coalition of the willing' to secure Ukraine if a ceasefire is reached. The United Kingdom is one of the five although it is not an EU member.

On Saturday 14 November, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, told reporters he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner said 'both sides', Kyiv and Moscow, know compromises will be needed to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff are working on next steps.

On Friday, Zelenskyy said US negotiators asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO. The report does not give his answer.
On Wednesday Zelenskyy said he did not believe it was possible to think about European security 'without Europe'.
The Kremlin said it is open to negotiations with Europe but criticised the bloc for a lack of proposals.
French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X on Saturday that Europe must clearly state what it wants for the period after the war, including to Russia, and that Ukraine belongs in NATO.
Putin, speaking during his Kremlin talks with Witkoff and Kushner, opposed any deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine after a peace deal, calling it 'absolutely unacceptable to us'.

The Abu Dhabi talks earlier in the week did not reach a breakthrough but produced a prisoner exchange; Zelenskyy said preparations are under way for what could be the largest prisoner exchange of the war.
Major differences remain over territory and future security guarantees.
Negotiators suggest another round of multilateral talks may follow, Al Jazeera's Mike Hanna reported.

stories.headline: COP31 Reaches Halfway With Limited Progress as Thousands March in Antalya and Ministers Arrive
stories.what_happened: The UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, reached its midpoint on Saturday 14 November with most formal agenda items still needing a lot of work. Thousands of campaigners marched through rainy streets calling for climate finance and an end to fossil fuels. Ministers arrive for the second week to settle the hardest issues, and a first draft of the main 'cover decision' is expected early in the week.
stories.why_it_matters: The second week is when countries must turn a long list of proposals into decisions, above all on who pays for climate action in poorer countries.

key_facts.fact: COP31 reached its midpoint on Saturday 14 November 2026; most formal agenda items 'still need a lot of work', Climate Home News reported.

Negotiations started on time and countries avoided a feared fight over the agenda, which UN climate chief Simon Stiell called 'constructive'. He urged governments to 'move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays'.
The cover text, the summit's main planned outcome, is still a wishlist of every proposal tabled; a first draft is expected early in the second week.

Thousands of campaigners from Turkish and international groups marched through rainy Antalya streets on Saturday, chanting 'no more blah blah blah - climate justice now!' and carrying dummy turtles, birds, polar bears and oil barrels.
Marchers demanded climate finance, a just transition for workers, an end to fossil fuels and protection for nature.
African countries want money for adapting to climate change tripled to 'at least $120 billion per year by 2035'.
Some large developing countries have pushed back all week on a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share to 35% of energy use by 2035; the pledge has at least 14 endorsements.
Some countries, including Arab nations, Mexico, Korea and Switzerland, proposed holding COP summits every two years instead of every year.
Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network said: 'Climate finance is the most important barrier to climate action in the Global South.'
Australia's Chris Bowen, who presides over the negotiations, said the shared presidency of Australia and Türkiye has worked 'exceedingly well'.
In the second week ministers arrive to take up and settle the most controversial issues, helped by pairs of countries.
A midway stocktaking plenary led by Türkiye and Australia was held on Saturday night, where countries were expected to set out their first red lines.

stories.headline: Southeast Asia's Leaders Open Their Summit in Manila, With Modi and Trump Due for Separate Meetings
stories.what_happened: The 49th ASEAN Summit opened in Manila on Sunday 15 November and runs to 17 November, closing the Philippines' year as chair of the 11-country group. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits the Philippines from 16 to 18 November for the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit, and US President Donald Trump is due at a separate ASEAN-US summit on Tuesday 17 November. Trade, defence and regional security are on the agenda.
stories.why_it_matters: Manila is the first stop in a week of summits in Asia that ends with the APEC meeting in China.

key_facts.fact: The 49th ASEAN Summit runs from 15 to 17 November 2026 in Manila; President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the leaders' meeting at the Philippine International Convention Center on Sunday 15 November.
ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, has 11 member states: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits the Philippines from 16 to 18 November, India's Ministry of External Affairs said, for the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit.
India's foreign ministry spokesperson said engagement with ASEAN is a key part of India's Act East Policy.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to attend a separate ASEAN-US Special Summit on Tuesday 17 November.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Marcos endorsed a framework committing both countries to pursue a free trade agreement by 2027.
Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said: 'The year brought unprecedented headwinds, particularly the crisis in the Middle East.'
After Manila, Marcos is scheduled to attend the APEC summit in China on 18 and 19 November.

The Philippines won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, held in Bangkok: Carmelle, 19 and the youngest contestant, won with the song 'Sobra-Sobra', beating performers from 10 other Asian countries with 211 points.

stories.headline: SpaceX Catches a Starship Upper Stage Returning From Orbit With Its Launch Tower's Arms, a First
stories.what_happened: On Saturday 14 November, SpaceX's Starship upper stage, Ship 42, returned from about 22 hours and 14 orbits in space and was caught in mid-air by the two mechanical arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas. Sources say no upper stage of an orbital rocket had been caught this way before. The Super Heavy booster from the same flight was not recovered after a low-fuel warning ended its catch attempt.
stories.why_it_matters: Catching the upper stage as well as the booster is a step towards rockets whose parts can all fly again, which could make spaceflight cheaper and more frequent.

key_facts.fact: Starship Flight 15 lifted off on the evening of Friday 13 November 2026 from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.
The upper stage, called Ship 42, completed about 14 orbits of Earth in roughly 22 hours, its longest orbital flight so far.
During the flight the ship released 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites into low Earth orbit.
On Saturday 14 November Ship 42 returned to Starbase and was caught by the launch tower's arms, the first time SpaceX has caught a Starship upper stage.
It was the first time an upper-stage rocket returning from orbit was caught and brought upright by its launch tower. The tower, nicknamed Mechazilla, uses two mechanical arms.
The ship was travelling at about 17,000 mph before the drag of the atmosphere slowed it.
To come home, the ship fired an engine to begin its descent, then faced extreme temperatures as it entered the atmosphere; black hexagonal heat-shield tiles protect it during this phase.
For the final descent, Ship 42 reignited three engines, turned to a vertical position and approached the tower, where two mechanical arms nicknamed 'chopsticks' secured it.
Two compact fittings near the top of the ship lined up with the tower's extended arms; the arms closed and held the vehicle several hundred feet above the ground, and the engines shut off.
It was SpaceX's fourth tower catch of Starship hardware; the three earlier catches involved only the Super Heavy booster.
The ship travels farther and faster than the booster and must survive the heat of re-entry from orbit, which makes catching it harder.

SpaceX had planned to recover both stages with the tower on this flight. The Super Heavy booster aborted its landing attempt after a low-fuel warning and came down in the Gulf of Mexico instead of being caught.
Flight 15 was the first attempt to catch both stages in one mission; only the ship succeeded, and the booster was not recovered.
SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said of the catch: 'That was the missing link.'

Recovering both stages could cut the time between missions, with SpaceX aiming to inspect, refurbish and relaunch vehicles faster. The heat shield still needs development before it can be reused with minimal refurbishment.
NASA's Artemis programme needs a modified Starship to serve as a lunar lander for crewed Moon missions.
SpaceX has not yet recovered both Starship stages on the same mission and will likely attempt that again on an upcoming flight.

stories.headline: A Depression in the Bay of Bengal Is Forecast to Become Cyclone Akvan and Head for the Andhra Pradesh Coast
stories.what_happened: A low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal strengthened into a depression on Sunday 15 November. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects it to become a cyclonic storm, to be named Akvan, on Monday 16 November, a severe cyclonic storm by 17 November, and to move northwest towards the Andhra Pradesh coast around 19 November. The IMD has warned of heavy rain in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal.
stories.why_it_matters: Several days of warning give coastal families, fishermen and officials time to prepare before the storm arrives.

key_facts.fact: The system developed from a low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal, which became a well-marked low early on Saturday 14 November 2026 and a depression on Sunday morning, 15 November.
In its Sunday bulletin the India Meteorological Department said the depression had moved north-northwestwards at 15 kmph over the previous six hours.

stories.headline: A Router Overload Halts Every US Flight Departure for More Than Four Hours; Recovery Takes the Whole Weekend
stories.what_happened: On Friday 13 November the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop, pausing all departures across the country for more than four hours after radar and communications at air traffic control centres became unstable. Officials traced it to a newly switched-on router at a remote site in El Dorado, Arkansas, part of work to replace copper lines with fibre; no cyberattack was found. More than 17,500 flights were cancelled on Friday and Saturday, nearly 2,300 more on Sunday, and officials expected normal operations by Monday 16 November.

key_facts.fact: Shortly after 3:30 p.m. Eastern time on Friday 13 November 2026 the FAA began experiencing 'instability for our radar and communications', Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
At 3:54 p.m. the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, pausing all departures across the country. Duffy said 3,500 planes were in the air at the time.
The ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m., after more than four hours.
Flights already in the air were allowed to reach their destinations; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said more than 3,000 aircraft landed safely during the disruption.
The FAA said all flights were halted 'out of an abundance of caution' and that every flight was accounted for. It said: 'Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems.'
It was only the second nationwide ground stop since 11 September 2001. The previous one was in 2023, when an FAA system that gives pilots safety notices before departure went down.
Instability hit 17 of the 22 en route air traffic control centres. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said none of the facilities actually went dark.
The problem first appeared as static at the Indianapolis centre. It took about 45 minutes to trace, partly because maintenance is logged on paper.
Nick Daniels, president of the air traffic controllers' union NATCA, said communications with some planes were disrupted and controllers moved flights to working radio frequencies.

The outage began with work to switch lines from copper to fibre at a remote FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Duffy said that when a new router there was turned on, a router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, installed about three weeks earlier, 'started to flood our system as well'.
Duffy said: 'Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data ... and started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.'

Officials believe a feature that broadcast data more widely than necessary caused the overload. The FAA has disabled it on all 69 routers of that type in the national airspace system, and Duffy said that resolved the issue.

Officials do not yet know whether the router was defective or whether the contractor, L3Harris, installed or configured it incorrectly. The FAA is working with the FBI, and both routers are being examined at an L3Harris lab in Florida.
The routers were made by Juniper, owned by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which said: 'the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly.'
Bedford said: 'We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related.' Officials found no evidence of a cyberattack.
L3Harris has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper to fibre, which Duffy says will be finished by the end of 2028.

Most days that week had about 100 flight cancellations in the United States.

Under US Transportation Department rules, a traveller whose flight is cancelled, or delayed by at least three hours, and who chooses not to fly is owed a full cash refund, even on a non-refundable ticket. Because the FAA ordered the stop, airlines generally do not owe meals or hotels for Friday's cancellations.
Several college football teams, including Auburn and Purdue, travelled to their games by bus instead of flying.
Cargo was also affected: US airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods a day, according to the industry group Airlines for America.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin Will Hold Their First Three-Way Meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November
stories.what_happened: The White House said on Friday 13 November, and the Kremlin confirmed on Saturday 14 November, that US President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin will meet together on Thursday 19 November in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Officials say Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and about the Iran war; Ukraine is not expected to be discussed. A senior US official said no agreement is expected and called the meeting the start of a conversation.

key_facts.fact: On Friday 13 November 2026 the White House said President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting will take place on Thursday 19 November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.
The Kremlin confirmed the meeting on Saturday 14 November.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russia's Tass news agency: 'This meeting will take place in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit.' The APEC summit runs on 18 and 19 November.
The White House called the three-way meeting 'unprecedented'.
Wales said: 'The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world.'
Trump says the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles.
A senior US official said the president 'does intend to talk about Iran' at the three-way meeting.
Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be discussed. The US official said Washington is running a separate negotiating track with Kyiv and Moscow, and that China is not part of that track.
A senior Trump administration official told Reuters: 'We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement.' The official described the meeting as the start of a conversation.
New START, the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow, lapsed in February 2026, nine months before the meeting.
With New START expired, the United States and Russia, which hold the largest atomic arsenals, have no limits on their stockpiles for the first time in more than 50 years.
Trump rejected Russia's proposal to extend New START by one year and demanded a 'new, improved and modernised' deal that includes China.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the United States, then China.
Pentagon estimates put China's arsenal above 600 warheads. The United States and Russia are each estimated to have more than 5,000.
China has shown little interest in a nuclear pact, given its much smaller stockpile.

Commentators have compared the planned meeting to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four occupation zones and finalised plans for the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the Yalta comparison, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on other countries.

Peskov said: 'It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant.' He added that a global order should rest on mutual benefit and mutual respect, not on any one power imposing its view.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.
Trump will also hold a separate working lunch and meeting with Xi on Thursday; it will be their fourth meeting since Trump returned to power last year.
Trump leaves Washington on Monday 16 November and arrives in the Philippines on Tuesday 17 November for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.
Elon Musk, the head of Tesla and SpaceX, will travel with Trump to China but will not take part in the meeting with Xi and Putin.
US export controls on sensitive chip technology are not expected to come up. A second US official said: 'We do not negotiate American export controls.'
The APEC summit brings 21 economies to Shenzhen, China's technology hub, which grew from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic centre in a few decades.
Analysts expect low odds of major breakthroughs and say the meeting will be more symbolic than substantive (Associated Press).
Trump and Putin have met in person seven times, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Putin have met more than 40 times since 2013.
China is Russia's top trading partner. China says it is neutral on the war in Ukraine.

The United States is at war with Iran; Trump and Xi have differed over it, and Russia has deepened its partnership with Iran. Analysts say the rise in global crude oil prices is mostly due to the Iran war.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said earlier that Russia and the US had not agreed on a separate two-way meeting between Putin and Trump on the sidelines.

stories.headline: Italy's Privacy Watchdog Fines Meta 805 Million Euros Over Facebook's Access to Android Photo Galleries
stories.what_happened: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta 805 million euros over a Facebook feature on Android phones that suggests photos and videos from the phone's gallery for posting. The authority found the feature was switched on by default and gave the app access to users' photos, videos and related data without specific, informed consent, affecting about 20 million Android users in Italy. Meta called the fine disproportionate and plans to appeal.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how European privacy law works in practice: an app must ask clearly before reading what is stored on someone's phone.

key_facts.fact: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta €805 million over the Facebook for Android app's feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for posting.
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($900 million) for accessing photos, videos and metadata on Italian users' Android devices without specific, informed consent.

The Garante found the feature was enabled by default and accessed Italian users' photos, videos and related metadata without explicit consent. It estimated about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected.

The app requested gallery access through one permission covering the whole app; a general notice did not clearly tell users they were also enabling gallery suggestions. Full access lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive.
The fine is about 0.47% of the group's global revenue.

The authority ruled under Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which applies the EU's ePrivacy rules: any access to data stored on a phone requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

Meta has 60 days to ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature and to keep the feature off by default, including for users who already granted permission. It must report to the authority within 30 days and again within 90 days.
Meta plans to appeal and called the fine 'disproportionate'. It said the feature 'works only after users give permission on their device' and that users can change this in settings at any time.
The investigation began in July 2025 after a complaint from a consumer group in Bolzano, Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti. The feature has been available since 2023.
The investigation did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI models; Meta denies such use.
In setting the penalty the authority weighed the large number of people affected, a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation.

Several college football teams, including Auburn and Purdue, travelled to their games by bus instead of flying.
Cargo was also affected: US airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods a day, according to the industry group Airlines for America.
Bedford said the network 'will continue to break until we replace it' and that there is 'no backup to the backup'. He apologised to travellers.

Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernise air traffic control. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy wants $50 billion; Duffy planned to send Congress a funding request on Monday 16 November.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, said Congress has given the administration what it asked for. Senator Maria Cantwell said the Senate Commerce Committee will review the communications technology problems.
Duffy said he expects the system to be 'back up and operational' for Thanksgiving travel. Thanksgiving was about a week away.
Daniels, the controllers' union president, said: 'I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things.' He noted that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases.
SpaceX launched its Starship test flight during the stop because the airspace near the Texas launch site had already been cleared.

stories.headline: SpaceX Catches a Starship Upper Stage Returning From Orbit With Its Launch Tower's Arms, a First
stories.what_happened: On Saturday 14 November, SpaceX's Starship upper stage, Ship 42, returned from about 22 hours and 14 orbits in space and was caught in mid-air by the two mechanical arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas. Sources say no upper stage of an orbital rocket had been caught this way before. The Super Heavy booster from the same flight was not recovered after a low-fuel warning ended its catch attempt.
stories.why_it_matters: Catching the upper stage as well as the booster is a step towards rockets whose parts can all fly again, which could make spaceflight cheaper and more frequent.

key_facts.fact: Starship Flight 15 lifted off on the evening of Friday 13 November 2026 from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.
The upper stage, called Ship 42, completed about 14 orbits of Earth in roughly 22 hours, its longest orbital flight so far.
During the flight the ship released 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites into low Earth orbit.
On Saturday 14 November Ship 42 returned to Starbase and was caught by the launch tower's arms, the first time SpaceX has caught a Starship upper stage.
It was the first time an upper-stage rocket returning from orbit was caught and brought upright by its launch tower. The tower, nicknamed Mechazilla, uses two mechanical arms.
The ship was travelling at about 17,000 mph before the drag of the atmosphere slowed it.
To come home, the ship fired an engine to begin its descent, then faced extreme temperatures as it entered the atmosphere; black hexagonal heat-shield tiles protect it during this phase.
For the final descent, Ship 42 reignited three engines, turned to a vertical position and approached the tower, where two mechanical arms nicknamed 'chopsticks' secured it.
Two compact fittings near the top of the ship lined up with the tower's extended arms; the arms closed and held the vehicle several hundred feet above the ground, and the engines shut off.
It was SpaceX's fourth tower catch of Starship hardware; the three earlier catches involved only the Super Heavy booster.
The ship travels farther and faster than the booster and must survive the heat of re-entry from orbit, which makes catching it harder.

SpaceX had planned to recover both stages with the tower on this flight. The Super Heavy booster aborted its landing attempt after a low-fuel warning and came down in the Gulf of Mexico instead of being caught.
Flight 15 was the first attempt to catch both stages in one mission; only the ship succeeded, and the booster was not recovered.
SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said of the catch: 'That was the missing link.'

Recovering both stages could cut the time between missions, with SpaceX aiming to inspect, refurbish and relaunch vehicles faster. The heat shield still needs development before it can be reused with minimal refurbishment.
NASA's Artemis programme needs a modified Starship to serve as a lunar lander for crewed Moon missions.
SpaceX has not yet recovered both Starship stages on the same mission and will likely attempt that again on an upcoming flight.

stories.headline: WHO Issues Its First Guidelines for Treating Adults With Type 1 Diabetes
stories.what_happened: On World Diabetes Day, 14 November, the World Health Organization published its first guidelines on diagnosing and managing type 1 diabetes in adults, written to work in all settings including places with few resources. They recommend insulin injections several times a day with doses adjusted to blood glucose, and regular glucose monitoring. WHO says about 9.5 million people lived with type 1 diabetes in 2025.
stories.why_it_matters: People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day to survive, and WHO wants everyone with the condition to have affordable insulin and glucose testing by 2030.

key_facts.fact: On 14 November 2026, World Diabetes Day, WHO issued its first guidelines on diagnosing and managing type 1 diabetes in adults, meant to apply in all settings, including low-resource, emergency and humanitarian ones.

Type 1 diabetes is a lifelong condition in which the body does not make enough insulin; people with it depend on daily insulin to survive. It was long seen mainly as a childhood condition but increasingly affects adults.
About 9.5 million people lived with type 1 diabetes globally in 2025, and about 500,000 people were diagnosed with it that year.

The guidelines recommend insulin injections several times a day, with doses adjusted to blood glucose levels, and regular monitoring: a finger-prick test or a continuous glucose monitor (a small sensor worn on the skin) at home.
Dr Søren Brostrøm of WHO said: 'Insulin is a lifesaving treatment, discovered more than 100 years ago.'
WHO's target is for everyone with type 1 diabetes to have access to affordable insulin and blood glucose self-monitoring by 2030.
In 2022, 830 million people had diabetes, most with type 2; more than 40% of people with diabetes do not know they have it.

stories.headline: A Depression in the Bay of Bengal Is Forecast to Become Cyclone Akvan and Head for the Andhra Pradesh Coast
stories.what_happened: A low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal strengthened into a depression on Sunday 15 November. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects it to become a cyclonic storm, to be named Akvan, on Monday 16 November, a severe cyclonic storm by 17 November, and to move northwest towards the Andhra Pradesh coast around 19 November. The IMD has warned of heavy rain in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal.
stories.why_it_matters: Several days of warning give coastal families, fishermen and officials time to prepare before the storm arrives.

key_facts.fact: The system developed from a low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal, which became a well-marked low early on Saturday 14 November 2026 and a depression on Sunday morning, 15 November.
In its Sunday bulletin the India Meteorological Department said the depression had moved north-northwestwards at 15 kmph over the previous six hours.
On Sunday morning the depression was about 800 km east-southeast of Chennai and 960 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam.
The IMD expects it to become a cyclonic storm on Monday 16 November, a severe cyclonic storm on 17 November, and it is 'likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm by November 19'.

After Monday the system is expected to move northwestwards towards the Andhra Pradesh coast. No direct landfall is expected over Tamil Nadu, though light to moderate rain is likely in parts of the state.
The system is forecast to move toward the Andhra Pradesh coast around 19 November; no landfall point or time has been given.
The IMD has warned of heavy rainfall over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal as the system intensifies.
Heavy rain is forecast in parts of West Bengal between 19 and 21 November, with the coastal districts of South 24 Parganas and Purba Medinipur most affected.
Fishermen and coastal communities have been told to follow official weather bulletins and warnings.
The storm will be named Akvan, a name given by Iran; it would be the third cyclone over the Bay of Bengal this season.

Background (how cyclones form): tropical cyclones typically form when conditions in the atmosphere are favourable and the sea surface temperature is above 26.5°C, according to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology.
Background (how cyclones form): over the ocean, low pressure systems cause warm, moist air to rise; clusters of thunderstorms can then form a band and start rotating around the low pressure area.

stories.headline: Before the 20 November UK-EU Summit, Lords Warn a Food and Farming Deal Would Mean Following Hundreds of EU Rules a Year
stories.what_happened: A House of Lords committee report published on 13 November, 'Dynamic alignment: a fundamental change', says the food and farming (SPS) agreement the UK government hopes to sign with the EU could bring at least 780 pieces of EU law a year for Parliament to scrutinise. Peers have asked the government to publish a fuller assessment of costs before the UK-EU summit on 20 November. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says a 'win-win' deal can be agreed and that it could lower prices; the government says the food deal will eventually bring 5.1 billion pounds in annual benefits.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal would remove most checks on food crossing between Britain and the EU, but in return the UK would keep following EU food rules it no longer votes on.

key_facts.fact: The House of Lords European Affairs Committee published a report titled 'Dynamic alignment: a fundamental change' on 13 November 2026. Its inquiry began in March 2026, received 70 written submissions and held 13 oral evidence sessions.
The committee's chair, Lord Stirrup, said the SPS agreement alone might generate at least 780 pieces of in-scope EU law a year, including technical and implementing matters.

Lord Stirrup said: 'This may sound like a technical issue, but the rules in question can affect everyday matters.' He said the rules affect food standards, consumer prices, business costs and household budgets.
The 780 figure counts EU legal acts in scope, including technical measures; it is not a count of new directives, and much of it is amendments to existing rules.
Dynamic alignment means the UK commits to keep pace with future EU rules in defined areas, rather than aligning once.
The SPS (sanitary and phytosanitary) agreement covers food and farming rules and would remove most checks. The EU insisted on dynamic alignment for it.
Under the arrangement the UK would have 'decision shaping' involvement but no decision-making vote, according to the House of Commons Library's account.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland, said a 'win-win' deal could be agreed, that it could lower consumer prices and business costs, and that talks would 'go down to the wire'.
The government says the food deal will eventually deliver £5.1 billion in annual benefits.
A UK-EU summit on 20 November is where the SPS agreement and a deal linking carbon-pricing schemes (ETS) are expected to be signed.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch opposes alignment; the Liberal Democrats called the draft deal a 'patch, not a fix'; Reform UK opposes alignment and the Greens favour closer integration.
The committee recommended a well-resourced system across government departments to track planned EU law, and a review of how Parliament scrutinises it.

Peers asked the government to publish a separate economic assessment of dynamic alignment before the UK-EU summit on 20 November, which is in Brussels. They said the GDP estimate leaves out financial contributions and compliance costs for businesses that do not trade with the EU.

The Fresh Produce Consortium, a trade body, warns that fruit and vegetables from outside the EU could face more than £300 million a year in extra costs if EU-style requirements and border checks are applied.

stories.headline: Europe Picks Five Countries to Sit at the Ukraine Peace Talks, and a US Envoy Offers to Arrange Europe-Russia Contact
stories.what_happened: At a summit in Dublin on Friday 13 November, European Council President António Costa announced that Europe will be represented in the Ukraine peace talks by the EU institutions plus five countries: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. On Saturday 14 November US envoy Jared Kushner said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move the talks to the next stage, including direct contact between Europe and Moscow. Ukraine's President Zelenskyy said US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas in exchange for joining NATO.
stories.why_it_matters: Europe has asked for months to be in the room where its own security is discussed; it now has a named team, though the hardest questions about territory are still open.

key_facts.fact: European Council President António Costa announced on Friday 13 November 2026, at a press conference after an informal European Council in Dublin, that the European negotiating team will consist of the EU institutions plus the 'E5': France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom.
Costa said: 'Our principles and our positions in these negotiations remain well known.' He said the team will act in unity and close coordination with all member states.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the team as 'E5 plus EU Institutions' and said: 'We will defend both Ukraine's and Europe's interests.' She also said: 'A strong European presence is important.'

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said these countries and the European institutions will negotiate with Russia, Ukraine and the US. He said: 'At stake are peace in Ukraine and the security of Poland and all of Europe,' and 'This is our time.'

Von der Leyen said the goal is to end the war with strong security guarantees and a plan for Ukraine's recovery, and that the EU will soon propose a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia and a way to close Ukraine's 2027 financing gap.

The five countries have signalled readiness to send troops in a 'coalition of the willing' to secure Ukraine if a ceasefire is reached. The United Kingdom is one of the five although it is not an EU member.

On Saturday 14 November, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, told reporters he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner said 'both sides', Kyiv and Moscow, know compromises will be needed to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff are working on next steps.

On Friday, Zelenskyy said US negotiators asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO. The report does not give his answer.
On Wednesday Zelenskyy said he did not believe it was possible to think about European security 'without Europe'.
The Kremlin said it is open to negotiations with Europe but criticised the bloc for a lack of proposals.
French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X on Saturday that Europe must clearly state what it wants for the period after the war, including to Russia, and that Ukraine belongs in NATO.
Putin, speaking during his Kremlin talks with Witkoff and Kushner, opposed any deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine after a peace deal, calling it 'absolutely unacceptable to us'.

The Abu Dhabi talks earlier in the week did not reach a breakthrough but produced a prisoner exchange; Zelenskyy said preparations are under way for what could be the largest prisoner exchange of the war.
Major differences remain over territory and future security guarantees.
Negotiators suggest another round of multilateral talks may follow, Al Jazeera's Mike Hanna reported.

stories.headline: Estonia Will Close Its Border Crossings With Russia From 1 December After a Foiled Arson Attack on a Drone Maker
stories.what_happened: Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced on Sunday 15 November that Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia from 1 December. The decision follows a failed attempt, in the early hours of 14 November, to break into and set fire to the premises of Threod Systems, an Estonian drone maker; Estonia's Internal Security Service says Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, ordered it. Eight suspects were detained. Russia denies responsibility for such operations.
stories.why_it_matters: A NATO and EU country is shutting its land border with Russia in response to what it calls a sabotage attempt, showing how tension from the war in Ukraine reaches other parts of Europe.

key_facts.fact: Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced on Sunday 15 November 2026, in a post on X, that Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points from 1 December.
Tsahkna said: 'Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.'
The decision followed a failed arson attack on 14 November 2026 against Threod Systems, an Estonian defence company that makes drones.
Estonia's Internal Security Service said the attack was ordered by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Suspects have been detained and criminal proceedings are under way.

In the early hours of 14 November, suspects tried to break into Threod Systems' premises in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, to cause an explosion and set the building on fire. The company's security staff and Estonian police prevented the attack, and significant damage was averted.
Eight Latvian citizens were detained.
Estonia has three road crossings with Russia: Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.
The government says the closure will limit Russia's ability to carry out hostile activities in Estonia and help prevent sanctions being dodged.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the operation aimed to frighten Estonia and undermine its support for Ukraine, and described it as part of Russia's wider 'hybrid warfare' against Europe.
Tsahkna said he had informed his counterparts in Finland, Latvia and Lithuania.
Russia denies responsibility for such operations.

An investigation by 17 European public broadcasters documented hundreds of reported hybrid incidents linked to Russia across 17 countries between 1 April and 15 October 2026, including arson, cyberattacks and suspicious drone activity.

stories.headline: Italy's Privacy Watchdog Fines Meta 805 Million Euros Over Facebook's Access to Android Photo Galleries
stories.what_happened: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta 805 million euros over a Facebook feature on Android phones that suggests photos and videos from the phone's gallery for posting. The authority found the feature was switched on by default and gave the app access to users' photos, videos and related data without specific, informed consent, affecting about 20 million Android users in Italy. Meta called the fine disproportionate and plans to appeal.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how European privacy law works in practice: an app must ask clearly before reading what is stored on someone's phone.

key_facts.fact: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta €805 million over the Facebook for Android app's feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for posting.
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($900 million) for accessing photos, videos and metadata on Italian users' Android devices without specific, informed consent.

The Garante found the feature was enabled by default and accessed Italian users' photos, videos and related metadata without explicit consent. It estimated about 20 million Android users in Italy were affected.

The app requested gallery access through one permission covering the whole app; a general notice did not clearly tell users they were also enabling gallery suggestions. Full access lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive.
The fine is about 0.47% of the group's global revenue.

The authority ruled under Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which applies the EU's ePrivacy rules: any access to data stored on a phone requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

Meta has 60 days to ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature and to keep the feature off by default, including for users who already granted permission. It must report to the authority within 30 days and again within 90 days.
Meta plans to appeal and called the fine 'disproportionate'. It said the feature 'works only after users give permission on their device' and that users can change this in settings at any time.
The investigation began in July 2025 after a complaint from a consumer group in Bolzano, Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti. The feature has been available since 2023.
The investigation did not examine whether gallery content was used to train AI models; Meta denies such use.
In setting the penalty the authority weighed the large number of people affected, a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation.
